title: Nepal takes government websites offline over critical PHP flaws - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal takes government websites offline over critical PHP flaws  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal’s government has temporarily taken its online systems offline to address two critical security flaws in PHP, a programming language used by nearly 70 percent of websites whose underlying technology can be identified.

The government began emergency security work on the evening of October 21 after the vulnerabilities became public. Some systems have since been patched and brought back online, according to the government’s Software Development and Operation Centre.

In a notice issued on Thursday , the centre, which operates under the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, said it had formed an emergency team with other technical centres and government representatives to secure affected systems. The team decided to take government systems offline as a precaution against possible breaches.

The centre said the shutdowns coincided with the Dashain holidays and had not affected government work. It aims to restore all critical systems after applying the necessary security updates.

The National Cyber Security Centre issued an urgent advisory on October 22, asking organisations to check their PHP installations and upgrade to patched versions. The warning covers not only websites running PHP directly but also platforms such as WordPress, Joomla, Drupal and Magento that rely on the technology.

The advisory does not establish that Nepali websites have been successfully attacked. It is a preventive measure intended to reduce the risk of unauthorised access.

What is PHP, and why does it matter?

PHP is an open-source programming language that runs on web servers. It works behind the scenes to generate the content users see when they open a website.

When someone visits a news website, for instance, the server may use PHP to retrieve the relevant article, assemble the page and send it to the visitor’s browser. Users generally do not see or interact with the underlying code.

PHP’s widespread use makes security flaws in the language particularly consequential. According to web technology tracker W3Techs , nearly 70 percent of websites whose programming language can be identified use PHP. The language also underpins WordPress, the content management system used by around 40 percent of websites worldwide, according to Reuters .

Its reach extends from personal blogs and small business websites to government portals, online shops and news platforms. Many website owners do not manage PHP themselves because the technology is built into the software or hosting services they use.

The figures do not mean that 70 percent of websites have been compromised. The actual risk depends on the PHP version running on a server, whether the relevant security updates have been installed and how the system is configured.

However, a flaw in a widely used component can expose a large number of systems to the same type of attack, making it difficult for organisations to assess and address their risks quickly.

What are the security flaws?

The two vulnerabilities have been assigned the identifiers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both received a severity score of 9.2 out of 10 under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, version 4.0, placing them in the critical category.

The principal concern is that an attacker could execute malicious code remotely on an affected server without first logging in or supplying a password.

The vulnerabilities involve PHP’s memory management and error-handling mechanisms. Under certain conditions, a specially crafted request can exploit weaknesses in how the software handles these processes, potentially allowing an attacker to execute commands on the server.

If exploited successfully, the flaws could give attackers access to sensitive information, allow them to alter website content or compromise the affected system more extensively. A compromised server could also become a foothold for further attacks.

The security risk prompted an urgent response from website operators and cybersecurity agencies, even though the discovery of a vulnerability does not in itself prove that a particular website has been breached.

Why were websites taken offline around the world?

Nepal’s response followed similar precautionary measures in other countries after the flaws were disclosed on October 21.

According to Reuters , government, school and hospital websites in several European countries were taken offline while their operators worked to apply security fixes. The countries affected included Germany, France, the Netherlands, Finland and the Czech Republic.

Other organisations also restricted access to online services. These included parts of Japan’s government services, websites operated by British public bodies and services run by the Wikimedia Foundation, which operates Wikipedia.

In Germany, a government spokesperson said the temporary shutdowns were precautionary and that no security incidents were known to have occurred at the time. Dutch public-facing websites, including hospital sites, were also taken offline as organisations followed cybersecurity guidance.

The response was driven by the possibility that attackers could exploit the flaws before operators had time to secure their systems. Taking a vulnerable service offline reduces its exposure to the public internet while updates are installed and verified.

The European Union’s cybersecurity agencies advised organisations to identify applications using PHP, coordinate with hosting providers and prioritise systems accessible from the internet. Where patches could not be applied immediately, they recommended isolating affected services until the risks could be addressed.

More recently, The Guardian reported that website operators had faced millions of attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities. Its report said major successful breaches had not been publicly identified, although the attempts highlighted the urgency of securing vulnerable systems.

What should Nepali website operators do?

The National Cyber Security Centre has directed organisations to upgrade their PHP installations to the latest patched releases appropriate to their systems.

The versions specified in its advisory are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35, or later releases in those branches.

The centre said PHP 8.1 and older versions do not have the required fixes available through the advisory and should be moved to a newer, secure version.

Organisations unable to apply the updates promptly have been advised to restrict public access to vulnerable services or isolate them from the internet until they can be secured.

The warning is relevant to government offices, media organisations, businesses and other institutions running their own websites. Those using third-party hosting services may also need to contact their providers to confirm which PHP version is in use and whether the security updates have been applied.

The immediate challenge is not simply installing a patch. Organisations must also identify every system running the vulnerable software, including applications that depend on PHP indirectly, and ensure that the updated version is actually running.

title: What’s new in the Nepal Premier League’s third season? - The Kathmandu Post
description: What’s new in the Nepal Premier League’s third season?  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The third season of the Nepal Premier League begins on October 26, bringing changes to how matches are officiated, how players’ performances are recorded and how spectators experience the tournament.

Billed as the “Festival of the Himalayas”, the competition runs until November 21 at the TU International Cricket Ground in Kirtipur. This season introduces the Decision Review System (DRS), follows the International Cricket Council’s sanction of the league and features a line-up of international stars alongside improvements to the stadium.

Here is what has changed and why it matters.

What does DRS mean for the NPL?

The biggest change on the field is the introduction of the Decision Review System, which allows teams to challenge certain umpiring decisions. The Cricket Association of Nepal has introduced the technology following controversies over decisions in previous editions.

The system will use three-dimensional ball tracking to review leg-before-wicket decisions, tracing the ball’s trajectory to assess whether it would have hit the stumps. Edge detection and sound-wave technology will help determine whether the ball made contact with the bat.

Video reviews will also cover run-outs, stumpings, front-foot no-balls, wides judged by height and measurements of sixes. Each team will be allowed two unsuccessful reviews per innings.

CAN secretary Paras Khadka says introducing the system will cost around Rs15 million to Rs20 million, with CAN and the eight franchises sharing the expense. As reviews are expected to add about 30 minutes to matches, the organisers have made an additional 30 minutes available in the initial schedule.

Why does ICC sanction matter?

On October 16, the ICC officially sanctioned the third season of the NPL. The significance goes beyond formal recognition: the matches in this edition will have official Twenty20 status.

That means runs and wickets recorded during the tournament will count towards players’ official career statistics. The sanction applies to the third season, rather than automatically covering future editions.

The absence of this status had made it harder for franchises to recruit active international players, particularly those from Test-playing nations. CAN had used a quota system to manage overseas recruitment under those circumstances. The sanction removes a significant obstacle to attracting such players.

What rules will overseas players have to follow?

The tournament will operate under anti-corruption measures, with the ICC’s Anti-Corruption Unit monitoring venues, dressing rooms and teams.

All overseas players, including retired cricketers, must obtain a no-objection certificate from their respective cricket boards. Players who have participated in an unauthorised private league during the six months before the NPL begins will not be eligible to play.

Each franchise can have six to eight overseas players in its squad. The playing XI, however, can include no more than four foreign players and must feature at least one player from an ICC Associate Member nation.

These requirements govern overseas recruitment and team selection while ensuring that Associate-member representation remains part of the competition.

Which international stars are playing this season?

International players have helped raise the league’s profile since its launch. India’s Shikhar Dhawan featured in the first edition, while South Africa’s Faf du Plessis played in the second.

This season’s confirmed signings include former Australia captain David Warner, who will represent Kathmandu Gorkhas, and West Indies power hitter Andre Russell, who has joined Biratnagar Kings. Bangladesh all-rounder Shakib Al Hasan will play for Pokhara Avengers.

Janakpur Bolts have signed England’s Moeen Ali and New Zealand’s Jimmy Neesham.

Former Pakistan fast bowler Shoaib Akhtar is also expected to visit Nepal for the tournament. He will not play but will work as an analyst for official broadcaster Himalaya Sports.

The presence of these players could give Nepali cricketers opportunities to learn from experienced international professionals while attracting more attention to the league abroad.

What has changed at the Kirtipur stadium?

CAN has also upgraded the TU International Cricket Ground to improve facilities for players, spectators and broadcasters.

The changes include around 2,000 additional seats, a covered stand and new seating. The ground has also been equipped with an LED scoreboard, digital perimeter boards, player dugouts with private dining facilities, a media centre, a dedicated family zone and improved toilet facilities.

The work is reported to be complete and the facilities ready for use. The upgrades are intended to improve the match-day experience and provide better facilities for international broadcasters and sponsors.

What will these changes mean for Nepali cricket?

The third season combines technological changes, official T20 status, high-profile overseas players and improved stadium facilities. Together, these developments could help raise the tournament’s profile and create more opportunities for Nepali players.

KATHMANDU - Nepal will receive US$20 million (S$25 million ) in aid from the United Nations' climate loss and damage fund after the devastating flood along its border with China’s Tibet region in August, the government said late on Thursday.

The Aug 26 flood killed about 1,500 people and more than 5,000 are still missing.

The flood affected about 60,000 people from 15,000 families, according to official data, and caused losses estimated at about US $2.7 billion to infrastructure including roads, bridges, schools and 13 hydropower plants.

Early official estimates show reconstruction bills could top US $4.7 billion.

The UN climate aid accounts for less than 1% of what Nepal needs to cover the cost of the flood.

The support from the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) was to "help address the severe damage caused by a climate-related disaster," the Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment said in a statement.

Nepal had sought the assistance in a letter to the FRLD in August, less than a week after the flood.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah, 36, in his maiden speech to the United Nations in September, said Nepal's disaster served as a warning to the world, and he blamed climate change for the flood despite his country's negligible emissions. REUTERS

title: FRLD approves $20 million grant for Nepal’s flood recovery - Khabarhub
description: FRLD approves $20 million grant for Nepal’s flood recovery  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) has approved a grant of US$20 million, equivalent to approximately Rs 3 billion, to support relief and reconstruction efforts in Nepal following devastating floods in the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river regions.

The grant was approved during a special meeting of the fund, according to the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment.

The Government of Nepal formally sought financial assistance on August 31 to address the extensive human and economic losses caused by the floods. The disaster affected more than 60,000 people across approximately 15,000 households.

Dr. Maheshwar Dhakal, joint secretary at the ministry, said the request was approved following extensive discussions among board members representing both developed and developing countries.

To receive the grant, Nepal must now submit a detailed project proposal outlining plans to assist communities affected by the floods.

Preliminary assessments indicate that the disaster claimed approximately 1,500 lives, while more than 5,000 people remain missing. Initial estimates put the economic damage at around US$2.7 billion, with total reconstruction costs projected to reach US$4.7 billion.

The approval marks an important step towards supporting Nepal’s recovery and strengthening the resilience of vulnerable communities facing climate-related disasters. It is also expected to contribute to broader efforts to advance climate justice, particularly for developing countries that bear significant losses from climate change despite having limited resources to respond.

Established under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the FRLD was agreed upon at COP27 and operationalized at COP28. The fund is designed to provide financial assistance to economically vulnerable developing countries experiencing climate-related losses and damage, including both economic and non-economic impacts.

title: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News - Khabarhub
description: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Economic Digest presents a brief yet comprehensive roundup of major business developments in Nepal, delivered in clear and accessible summaries.

The reports highlight Nepal’s economic and developmental challenges, particularly the need to balance employment, agricultural sustainability, infrastructure development, and disaster resilience. The continued departure of young Nepalis for foreign employment reflects limited domestic job opportunities and low wages. Although remittances support household incomes, sustained labour migration could weaken agricultural productivity and industrial growth.

Meanwhile, Mustang’s buckwheat farming demonstrates the potential of traditional agriculture to strengthen local livelihoods, preserve indigenous food systems, and attract tourism through improved market connectivity. Nepal’s declining tea exports reveal the risks of excessive dependence on a single market, emphasizing the importance of export diversification, reliable quality testing, and stronger institutional support. Infrastructure initiatives, including the reconstruction of four suspension bridges, offer opportunities to improve connectivity and community access.

However, Myagdi’s reconstruction funding shortages expose weaknesses in disaster preparedness and local financial capacity. Overall, sustainable development requires coordinated policies that expand domestic employment, modernize agriculture, diversify exports, strengthen infrastructure, and improve disaster-response financing.

TIA sees continued departure of Nepali youth for foreign employment

Hundreds of young Nepalis continued to leave the country through Tribhuvan International Airport (TIA) in search of overseas employment, higher education, and other international opportunities, even as families across Nepal celebrated the Dashain festival. International departure terminals remained crowded with young job seekers and professionals heading abroad amid limited domestic employment opportunities, low wages, and inadequate economic incentives. Although remittances sent by Nepalis working overseas remain essential to household finances, community observers have raised concerns about the growing departure of the country’s working-age population. They warn that sustained labour migration could undermine agricultural productivity, reduce the industrial workforce, and weaken economic stability in rural communities over the long term.

Mustang farmers begin harvesting traditional buckwheat crops

Farmers throughout Mustang district are harvesting traditional buckwheat cultivated on terraced fields at elevations ranging from 2,000 to 5,000 metres above sea level. The nutritious crop is an important part of the region’s traditional high-altitude farming system, alongside local barley, naked oats, and potatoes. Buckwheat is grown across all five local administrative units, from Thasang-1 in Tukche to settlements near the border around Lo Manthang. It thrives in upland fields and open spaces within apple orchards, tolerates cold conditions, and generally matures in around 100 days. The harvest supplies local households while also serving regional commercial markets. Improved road connectivity has made it easier to transport buckwheat products to other areas. Traditional foods prepared from buckwheat flour, including rotis and other local specialities, have also become popular culinary attractions for domestic and international visitors exploring the Himalayan region.

Nepal’s tea sector seeks stable markets as exports decline

Nepal’s tea industry is facing increasing market uncertainty despite having a strong production base. Exporters are urging improvements in quality testing, diversification of export destinations, and greater government support. Tea exports through the Kakarbhitta border point declined by 14.8 percent to 13,045 metric tons in fiscal year 2025/26, while their total value fell by 15.3 percent to Rs 3.529 billion. India accounts for 86 percent of Nepal’s tea exports, making the industry highly vulnerable to fluctuations in demand and changes in trade procedures. Revised tea-testing requirements introduced by India further complicated exports, forcing 83 tea factories in Ilam and Jhapa to temporarily suspend production in May and June 2026. Although the regulations were subsequently amended, exporters remain concerned about additional costs and delays. Industry stakeholders emphasize the need for dependable testing laboratories, stronger assistance for pesticide-free tea production, and greater access to international markets to ensure fair returns for farmers and sustainable industry growth.

More than 3,500 citizens use free police bus services during Dashain in Kathmandu

A total of 3,585 people used free shuttle bus services provided by Nepal Police and the Armed Police Force across the Kathmandu Valley during the Dashain holidays. The initiative was introduced to make travel easier and more affordable during the major festive period. Official records show that Nepal Police carried 1,406 passengers using three dedicated buses on Maha Nawami and Bijaya Dashami. Meanwhile, the Armed Police Force operated two vehicles and transported 2,179 passengers over several days, with the service concluding on Friday. Passengers welcomed the annual initiative for offering safe and free transportation during the busy festival period. The service also helped protect commuters from excessive fares charged by private public transport operators in the capital region.

Myagdi struggles to secure funds for post-disaster reconstruction

Local governments in Myagdi district are facing serious financial constraints as they attempt to rebuild infrastructure and rehabilitate communities affected by destructive monsoon floods and landslides. The disasters caused significant infrastructure damage and loss of life, increasing the need for urgent reconstruction and relief efforts. Persistent heavy rainfall damaged rural roads, suspension bridges, drinking water pipelines, irrigation canals, and electricity transmission lines, leaving several remote settlements isolated. Municipal representatives say the available disaster management reserves are insufficient to cover even essential repairs and have appealed to federal and provincial governments for additional financial assistance. Community fundraising efforts and contributions through salary deductions have also begun to support recovery work. However, damaged electricity networks and disrupted road access in several remote wards continue to obstruct daily travel, service delivery, and local economic activities.

Electrical short circuit causes fire damage exceeding Rs 15 million in Banke

A fire at Amber Steel in Bakaspur, Janaki Rural Municipality-5, Banke, caused property damage estimated at more than Rs 15 million. The blaze broke out inside the facility’s furnace oil storage tank enclosure at approximately 1:30 a.m., with preliminary reports identifying an electrical short circuit in the industrial wiring as the cause. According to the District Police Office, local police personnel, regional fire engines, and community members responded to the incident. Their coordinated efforts brought the fire under control within about an hour, preventing it from spreading further and causing additional damage to nearby manufacturing units within the steel production complex.

Four suspension bridges to be rebuilt under the Tanahun Hydropower Project

Tanahun Hydropower Limited has signed a contract with a Kathmandu-based joint venture contractor to reconstruct four suspension bridges affected by the reservoir area of the 140-megawatt Tanahun Hydropower Project. The contract is worth Rs 160 million, excluding applicable taxes, and is intended to restore reliable transportation links for communities affected by reservoir submergence. Following consultations with local residents, replacement sites were selected for the bridges at Chulesi, Tunibote, Dhwang, and Tutuwa. Construction materials and equipment have already been transported to the sites to facilitate the work. The project aims to complete the reconstruction of all four bridges before mid-2028, helping restore essential connections between local settlements.

title: Loss and Damage Fund approves $20 million grant for Nepal’s flood recovery - Onlinekhabar English
description: Loss and Damage Fund approves $20 million grant for Nepal’s flood recovery  Onlinekhabar English
publisher.title: Onlinekhabar English
full_article:
Kathmandu, October 23

The Loss and Damage Fund, established to address climate-related losses and damages, has approved a $20 million grant for Nepal to support relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction in communities affected by devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river basins.

The Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment announced the decision in a statement on Thursday, saying the funding would support families and communities affected by the floods that struck on August 26.

The disaster has claimed more than 1,500 lives, while over 5,000 people remain missing, according to the ministry. More than 60,000 people from approximately 15,000 households have been directly affected.

Preliminary estimates put the economic damage caused by the floods at around $2.7 billion, equivalent to Rs 407.7 billion. Reconstruction costs are estimated at approximately $4.7 billion, or Rs 709.7 billion.

Nepal’s request receives international backing

To accelerate assistance to flood-affected communities, Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle and Agriculture Minister Geeta Chaudhary made a special appeal to the fund’s board on August 31.

Following the request, formal and informal discussions took place in several rounds among board members representing developed and developing countries, least developed countries, small island developing states, and regional groups from Asia-Pacific, Africa, Latin America and Western countries.

A special board meeting held on October 22 finalised the decision to provide assistance to Nepal, said Dr Maheshwar Dhakal, joint secretary at the ministry.

Dhakal, who also serves as the ministry’s spokesperson, coordinated Nepal’s engagement with the fund and facilitated the process.

Nepal will now prepare and submit a proposal to the fund under the Barbados Implementation Modalities process to access the approved financing.

The ministry also announced that the fund’s 11th board meeting will be held in Kathmandu from March 17 to 19, 2027.

Historic step for climate finance

Dhakal, Nepal’s national focal point to the fund and an alternate board member, described the grant approval as a landmark development in the country’s efforts to secure international climate finance.

“There could hardly be a more important and historic decision in Nepal’s climate finance history,” he said, adding that the approval also marked a new chapter in the history of the Loss and Damage Fund itself.

He welcomed the international community’s decision to prioritise the severe human and economic losses caused by flooding in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river basins.

The grant is expected to contribute to recovery efforts in affected communities, although Nepal must complete the proposal process before the funds can be disbursed.

title: Nepal experiences post-monsoon conditions - Khabarhub
description: Nepal experiences post-monsoon conditions  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Nepal is currently experiencing post-monsoon weather conditions, with westerly winds and local weather systems continuing to influence weather patterns across the country.

According to the Weather Forecasting Division, the hilly and mountainous regions are expected to experience partly cloudy skies, while most parts of the Tarai are likely to remain predominantly clear.

The Division has forecast the possibility of isolated light rainfall and snowfall in some hilly and mountainous areas. Weather conditions may vary by location, particularly in higher-altitude regions where local atmospheric changes can bring cloud cover and precipitation.

The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology confirmed that the monsoon system completely withdrew from Nepal on October 14, marking the transition to the post-monsoon season. However, the departure of the monsoon does not mean an end to all rainfall, as local weather systems and westerly winds can continue to influence conditions across the country.

Post-monsoon weather generally brings clearer skies and less widespread rainfall, although localized precipitation and snowfall remain possible, particularly in the hills and mountains.

Residents and travellers, especially those planning journeys to mountainous destinations, are advised to monitor the latest weather bulletins for updates on changing conditions that could affect travel and outdoor activities.
